fatal_errors: The proposed mediator—fine, ductile intergranular secondary phases—is not supported by the reported structure, which consists of solidification-segregated W-Ta-rich dendrites and Zr-Ti-rich interdendritic regions forming two BCC phases.

Grain-boundary sliding and enhanced dislocation mobility were not established as the governing mechanisms; the reported interpretation instead emphasized solid-solution/lattice-distortion strengthening and Ti-V-Zr-related effects on dislocation cores, cohesion, localized plasticity, and crack propagation.
No prior evidence is cited despite the explicit request for cited support.
The assumed fully recrystallized, grain-size-matched initial states replace the actual comparison between an as-cast alloy and coarse-grained powder-sintered commercial tungsten.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the correct property contrast and predicts greater plastic strain and toughness than pure tungsten, so it is aligned at a broad level. However, it reconstructs neither the actual material states nor the controlled compression, temperature-dependent indentation, and scratch-toughness measurements. Its central causal claim relies on unobserved ductile grain-boundary phases and grain-boundary sliding, whereas the observed mediator was a dendritic two-BCC-phase segregation structure. The proposed matched-grain-size testing with microscopy is testable and could evaluate whether such phases exist, but post-mortem correlation would not by itself isolate their causal role; a stronger test would manipulate phase morphology or grain-boundary coverage independently. Conditions and validity limits are vague, and irradiation or simulated plasma exposure was not part of the reported evidence. With no cited supporting evidence and a mediator inconsistent with characterization, this is an unsupported alternative rather than a reconstruction.
